speaker_role: current admissions officer (Associate Dean for Admissions, Dartmouth Geisel School of Medicine)
commercial_incentive: Yes - podcast produced by 'Accepted' (an admissions consulting company), promotes their paid quiz/consulting throughout
key_insights: This entire interview concerns MD (medical school) admissions at Geisel, not US undergraduate admissions, so it is off-scope for an undergraduate admissions knowledge base
Geisel screens applicants only on a minimum MCAT score of 503 (disclosed publicly on their website) and otherwise does full holistic review with no further hard screen

Interviews are conducted virtually (two 30-minute one-on-one sessions) year-round on a rolling admissions basis into early March, and the school found no difference in admit rates between in-person and virtual interview cohorts

Dean advises secondary-essay writers to explain how a described experience changed their thinking/perspective rather than just recounting the event, and to avoid repeating content already in the activities section

Dean states she is not concerned about ChatGPT-written essays because file 'synchrony' (consistency between personal statement, emails, and interview persona) reveals inauthenticity regardless of the writing tool used

Community college prerequisites are accepted as long as they meet Geisel's requirements; shadowing and other clinical experiences (EMT, nursing, pharmacy work) are treated interchangeably under a broad 'clinical experience' umbrella
Dean warns against inflated or implausible reported activity hours (e.g. claiming thousands of hours that don't fit a full course load), saying reviewers check whether the math is plausible
Received about 7,000 applications for 92 seats in the cited admissions cycle (Geisel's largest class ever)
specific_numbers_or_facts: Geisel's minimum MCAT screening threshold stated as 503
Geisel had about 7,000 applicants for 92 seats (90 MD, 2 MD-PhD) in the cycle discussed
Interview invitations continue rolling out into early March; prior cycle's interviewing reportedly stopped around March 14th
Three of four required secondary essay questions reportedly have no word limit
